overview.text: The Interstate Highway System is the federally supported network of major highways formally named the National System of Interstate and Defense Highways. Its origins predate the 1956 law: a 1944 act called for a national network connecting major cities and industrial centers while serving national defense, but construction lacked dedicated funding. On June 29, 1956, President Dwight D. Eisenhower signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act, which expanded the planned system to 41,000 miles, established the Highway Trust Fund, and assigned the federal government 90 percent of project costs. Designed to uniform standards, Interstates feature controlled access—drivers enter and exit at designated points—and generally have at least two lanes in each direction. They serve military and civilian travel alike.

key_facts.text: The Interstate idea developed before Eisenhower’s presidency: the 1944 Federal-Aid Highway Act called for a national system of up to 40,000 miles.
Eisenhower signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act on June 29, 1956; it increased the proposed system to 41,000 miles.
The 1956 law created the Highway Trust Fund, using federal motor-vehicle taxes to support highway construction, and set the federal share of Interstate project costs at 90 percent.
The 1956 act called for uniform design standards, including full control of access and a minimum of two travel lanes in each direction.
Eisenhower’s experience in a 1919 U.S. Army transcontinental convoy and his observations of German autobahns helped shape his support for better highways.
